name: Home in Orbit: Stations, Shuttles and Their Crews
description: From Laika and Gagarin to Salyut, Skylab, Mir, the Shuttle and the International Space Station: how people learned to live and work in orbit.

checkpoints.name: First flights
checkpoints.note: Laika the dog went up in 1957, and NASA's Project Mercury and the Soviet programme followed. Yuri Gagarin became the first person in orbit in 1961, and Valentina Tereshkova the first woman in 1963.

checkpoints.name: The first stations
checkpoints.note: Salyut 1 was the first space station, launched in 1971; one crew, flown up in a Soyuz capsule, lived aboard but died on the way home. Skylab, launched by NASA in 1973, gave three American crews a workshop in orbit, though it eventually fell back to Earth in 1979.

checkpoints.name: The shuttle arrives
checkpoints.note: The Space Shuttle flew into orbit and landed like a plane. Sally Ride became the first American woman in space in 1983, and Svetlana Savitskaya was the first woman to walk in space in 1984.

checkpoints.name: Mir, Hubble and loss
checkpoints.note: The loss of Challenger in 1986 killed its crew, including teacher Christa McAuliffe. The Soviet Mir station was a home for years, the Hubble Space Telescope was released from a shuttle, and John Glenn flew again in 1998 as work on the ISS began.

checkpoints.name: The station years
checkpoints.note: The International Space Station has hosted crews continuously since 2000, including Peggy Whitson. The Columbia disaster in 2003 grounded the shuttles, and China's Shenzhou 5 made it the third country to send a person into orbit.
